teaser: Munch scratched and scraped this canvas for a year. Then the public laughed at it.
review_notes:
Fellow painter Gustav Wentzel reportedly calling Munch a 'humbug painter' at the 1886 opening: widely repeated anecdote, check.
Model Betzy Nielsen, age 11, met during a house call with Munch's father: check.
Six painted versions between 1885-86 and 1927: check count.
Tate version removed from Dresden by the Nazis and sold in 1939: check.
Munch's remark that most of his later work was born in this picture is paraphrased, not quoted.

lesson.text: This canvas was painted for one particular wall: the Autumn Exhibition of 1886 in Kristiania, the city now called Oslo. It was the big yearly show where Norwegian painters proved what they could do. The fashion there was naturalism, which means painting things exactly as the eye sees them, down to every button and floorboard.

Edvard Munch was 22 and hung his picture among those polished canvases under a modest title: “Study.” It shows a sickroom. A red-haired girl sits propped against a big white pillow. A woman beside her has let her head drop. Almost nothing else is clear.

Munch knew this room by heart. In 1877 his older sister Sophie died of tuberculosis at 15. He was 13. Their mother had died of the same disease when he was five. He was not painting a girl he had observed. He was painting a memory that had been with him for nine years.

lesson.title: Two people, one grief
lesson.text: Three places carry the whole scene. Follow them from the girl to the woman to the point where they meet.

spots.title: The profile
spots.text: Her face is pale against the pillow and turned away from the woman. She looks toward the right, where the light seems to come from. There is no fear in it, only tiredness.

spots.title: The bowed head
spots.text: We never see the woman's face, just the top of her dark hair. She cannot look at the child. It is the adult, not the patient, who has given up.

spots.title: The hands
spots.text: Their hands meet at the exact center of the canvas, but they dissolve into one pale smear. Munch painted the touch and left out the fingers.

lesson.text: Notice who is comforting whom. The dying girl sits upright and calm, while the grown woman collapses. Munch turned the usual sickbed picture around. Many painters of the 1880s showed pale children in bed, in neat detail. Critics even called it “the pillow period.” None of them looked like this.

The girl was not Sophie, of course. Munch's model was an 11-year-old named Betzy Nielsen, whom he is said to have noticed while following his father, a doctor, on a house call. His aunt Karen, who had raised the Munch children, posed as the grieving woman.

He worked on the canvas for about a year. He painted the scene, scraped it off, painted it again, let thinned paint run down, and scored the wet layers with a knife or the wooden end of his brush. He said he was trying to get back the first impression: the trembling mouth, the transparent skin, the tired eyes.
So the damage you see is the method. The surface is a record of all the versions he destroyed on the way. One small object survived the scraping almost intact, and it sits far from the two figures.
Somewhere in the dark there is a drinking glass, half full. Can you tap it?

spots.title: The glass
spots.text: A glass with something red in it stands in the lower right corner, perhaps medicine. It is one of the few objects with a clear outline, and it echoes the reddish table and bottle on the far left.

lesson.text: The glass on one side and a bottle on a table on the other frame the bed like two quiet reminders of months of nursing. Between them, everything is blur. That is how a room looks through tears, or through a memory you have gone over too many times.

At the opening, visitors laughed out loud in front of the picture. One fellow painter is said to have called Munch a “humbug painter” to his face. Newspapers described the canvas as unfinished, a mess of half-rubbed-out sketching.
Munch stopped painting what a scene looks like and painted what it felt like to be there. The scratches and blur are not mistakes. They are the feeling.

One person in Kristiania defended him: the painter Christian Krohg, his older friend and teacher. Munch gave him the canvas. It later entered Norway's national collection, where it hangs today as the picture that started everything for him.

spots.title: Scored paint
spots.text: Above the pillow, thin vertical lines run through the paint like rain on a window. Munch scratched them into the wet surface.

spots.title: The pillow
spots.text: A huge white pillow rises behind the girl's red hair like a pale halo. It is the brightest area of the canvas and pushes her profile forward.

spots.title: The table
spots.text: A red-brown bedside table with a hazy bottle on top. Its warm color is answered by the red in the glass at the opposite corner.

spots.title: The blanket
spots.text: The gray-green blanket is all long sweeping strokes, with no folds drawn. It fills almost half the picture with restless movement.

spots.title: The curtain
spots.text: A dark green curtain closes the right edge. The girl's gaze goes this way, toward a window we never see.

spots.title: Signature
spots.text: Munch signed and dated the canvas in the lower left corner, in thin red strokes that almost sink into the paint.

lesson.text: Munch could not let the subject go. Over the next forty years he painted it again and again, six canvases in all, the last in 1927, and made prints of it too. One version, once in a Dresden museum, was removed by the Nazis as “degenerate” and is now at Tate in London.
Late in life Munch said that most of what he did afterward was born in this picture. The Scream came seven years later. Its wavering sky makes more sense once you have stood in this room first.

quiz.question: Whose death was Munch remembering when he painted this scene?
quiz.explanation: Sophie died of tuberculosis in 1877, at 15.

quiz.question: Under what title did Munch first show the picture in 1886?
quiz.explanation: He exhibited it simply as “Study” at the Autumn Exhibition.

quiz.question: How did Munch get the worn, streaked surface?
options: The canvas was damaged in a fire
He scraped, repainted and scratched the paint for about a year
He painted it in one afternoon with a sponge
quiz.explanation: The surface records a year of scraping, repainting and scoring.

quiz.question: Which figure hides her face?
quiz.explanation: The woman bows her head so that only her dark hair shows.

quiz.question: Who defended the painting and received it as a gift?
quiz.explanation: Krohg, Munch's older friend and teacher, stood up for it.

facts.text: Munch painted the subject of the sick child only once.
facts.explanation: He returned to it for forty years, painting six versions.

facts.text: Visitors laughed at the painting when it was first shown.
facts.explanation: The 1886 public saw it as an unfinished mess.

facts.text: The girl who posed was Munch's sister Sophie.
facts.explanation: Sophie had died nine years earlier; the model was Betzy Nielsen.
